episode_title: Make $6,000 or Close: A 19-Year-Old's Last Chance at Saving Her Art Studio in Singapore (ft. SCURO)

real_qa.q: Why did SCURO pivot from horror art jamming to neon experiences?
real_qa.r: After opening in October during Halloween, the horror art jamming studio had good initial bookings but then experienced a sharp decline. Merida needed to pivot quickly to pay rent. Through talking to customers and understanding what they truly wanted, she discovered that birthday parties and team bonding were not unique products, but she could differentiate through marketing and customer experience. The winning product became neon experiences, which leveraged her existing strengths with kids and face painting.
real_qa.requete: SCURO pivot horror art neon experiences

real_qa.q: How did a 19-year-old school dropout build business acumen to launch and pivot SCURO?
real_qa.r: Merida developed her skills by getting her hands dirty and doing the work herself, talking directly with customers and parents to understand their needs. She hosted hundreds of birthday parties and taught art classes to learn what needed to be done before training her team. She also emphasized that she is mediocre at many things, but her superpower is being mediocre at everything, which allows her to understand diverse aspects of the business and hire people smarter than herself in areas where she is weak.
real_qa.requete: school dropout business skills SCURO founder

real_qa.q: What did Merida mean by posting the $6,000 TikTok ultimatum for SCURO?
real_qa.r: At 19 years old with very little savings left, Merida posted a TikTok saying she would close SCURO if she did not make $6,000 in 30 days. She described this as her last resort to get money or virality, with the philosophy that if she was going to fail, she would fail with a bang by trying her hardest rather than closing down quietly. Her bigger fear was not business failure but staying somewhere she did not want to stay for the next 30 or 40 years of her life.

real_qa.q: How does SCURO ensure quality and reliability with over 20 part-time student staff?
real_qa.r: SCURO uses a selective hiring process, choosing outgoing people with energy for kids parties who can also set boundaries and be responsible. The pay structure is $12 base per hour plus $4 incentive per hour for hitting milestones like not cancelling shifts, showing up on time, and getting good reviews. This creates strong incentive for reliability. They also have training systems and quality matrices in place to ensure parents can trust the experience at every kids party.

real_qa.q: What skills did Merida struggle with in building SCURO and how did she address them?
real_qa.r: Merida acknowledged being weak at numbers and monotonous tasks like accounting and admin work, which she described as possibly related to an ADHD brain. Rather than forcing herself to perform these tasks poorly, she focused on her strengths—working with kids and marketing—while outsourcing admin work. She emphasized the importance of hiring A-star or overcompetent employees rather than settling for good enough, acknowledging she is not the best at everything and needs people smarter than her in specific areas.
real_qa.requete: SCURO founder weakness admin hiring overcompetent

guest.bio_context: Merida is a 19-year-old school dropout who founded SCURO, a neon art jamming studio in Singapore, after initially starting with a horror art jamming concept. She pivoted her business model when the original offering did not generate sufficient revenue, eventually discovering that neon experiences for birthday parties and team bonding were her winning product. She has built SCURO to operate two studio locations with over 20 part-time staff and has gained media attention including coverage in The Straits Times.

real_quote: If I'm going to fail, at least let it be with a bang. I tried my hardest and I did the very best I could with what I had.
